Estimate a latency network analysis model

Source: R/build_aliases.R
build_latency.Rd

build_network(method = "latency"), or for short build_latency(), estimates a latency network analysis model from a message log. The edge from sender A to sender B is the average weight of A's replies to B, each reply weighted by its speed: 1 for an immediate reply, falling linearly to floor at cap (Templeton et al., 2022).

Its edges are the replies of build_reverse(): within each sequence (an actor's events, split by session or time_threshold), each event points from its sender, the responder, to the sender of the event before it. A reply that takes \(t\) seconds weighs \(1 - (1 - f) \min(t / c, 1)\), with \(f\) the floor and \(c\) the cap in seconds, and the weights of a pair are averaged, or summed with aggregate = "sum". A sender who posts twice in a row is a self-loop on the diagonal, weighted by the same rule. Shifting every time by a constant leaves the weights unchanged, and so does a change of time unit when the cap is a percentile. extract_edges() adds each edge's number of replies (n_replies) and their median latency in seconds (median_latency). start, end and params = list(weighted = TRUE) raise an error of class nestimate_bad_input. bootstrap_network() resamples latency networks by their sequences and judges stability on the speed score; the other resampling verbs, such as permutation(), raise an error of class nestimate_latency_resampling on one.

In build_network() the four settings are named latency_floor, latency_cap, latency_aggregate and latency_scope.

Usage

build_latency(
  data,
  action,
  time,
  actor = NULL,
  session = NULL,
  order = NULL,
  time_threshold = 900,
  timezone = "UTC",
  floor = 0.5,
  cap = 0.95,
  aggregate = c("mean", "sum"),
  scope = c("global", "actor", "session", "responder"),
  group = NULL,
  scaling = NULL,
  threshold = 0,
  labels = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

data

A message log: one row per message, action the sender.

action

The column holding each message's sender.

time

The timestamp column. Events are ordered by it, and a gap longer than time_threshold starts a new sequence.

actor

The column naming who each row belongs to (a person, a team). In an event log, each actor's events form a sequence, split further by session or time_threshold; in one-hot data, each actor's rows. Default NULL.

session

The column identifying sessions in an event log; each session is its own sequence, also without actor. Default NULL.

order

The column that orders events sharing a timestamp; without it, those events keep their row order. Default NULL.

time_threshold

The longest gap, in seconds, between two events of the same sequence in an event log; a longer gap starts a new sequence. FALSE turns the split off, so each actor (or actor-session) is one sequence. Default 900.

timezone

The Olson time zone for timestamps without an offset (passed to prepare()); timestamps with an offset, such as ...Z or +02:00, are converted from it. Default "UTC".

floor

The weight of a reply that takes cap or longer, a single number from 0 to 1. 1 ignores time (with aggregate = "sum", the counts of build_reverse()); 0 gives replies at or past the cap no weight. Default 0.5.

cap

The time at which a reply's weight reaches floor. A number in (0, 1] is a percentile of the latencies of the replies to another sender, pooled over all of data (with group, over every group, so the groups share one cap); a string such as "120s" is a number of seconds. The resolved cap, in seconds, is stored on the network. Default 0.95.

aggregate

How the replies of a pair of senders make one weight: "mean" (default) averages their weights, the pair's typical reply speed; "sum" adds them, so an edge grows with both the speed and the number of replies.

scope

With a percentile cap: the units that get their own cap. "global" (default) takes one cap from all of data; "actor" one per value of actor; "session" one per sequence; "responder" one per responding sender. A unit with fewer than 5 replies to another sender takes the global cap, and a message of class nestimate_latency_fallback says how many units did. A cap in seconds applies to every reply, so a scope other than "global" is then ignored with a message of class nestimate_ignored_argument.

group

A column to split the data by: one network per value, returned as a netobject_group. Default NULL.

scaling

Rescaling applied to the weights after estimation, in the order given: "minmax" rescales the weights to run from 0 to 1, over every cell for the transition methods (tna's rule, so with no zero cell the smallest weight becomes 0) and over the non-zero weights, into (0, 1], for the other methods, "max" divides by the largest absolute weight, "rank" replaces the non-zero weights by their ranks, and "normalize" makes each row's absolute weights sum to 1; an undirected network whose matrix it makes asymmetric becomes directed, so both of a pair's values are kept as edges. Zero weights stay zero under every option. Combine them as in c("rank", "minmax"). Default NULL (none).

threshold

Weights whose absolute value is below this are set to zero. Default 0 (none).

labels

New display labels for the nodes, applied after estimation: a two-column data frame (name, label), a named character vector c(name = "label") or a named list. It rewrites the node labels and the weight matrix's dimnames; nodes not listed keep their names. Default NULL.

...

Further arguments for build_network(): prepare()'s time options unix_time_unit, is_unix_time and custom_format. method cannot be given (error of class nestimate_bad_input).

Value

A netobject (a netobject_group with group), as build_network() returns it. Beside the weights it keeps initial, n_replies and median_latency (matrices laid out as the weights), latency_cap_seconds (the resolved global cap), latency_unit_caps (the per-unit caps of a non-global scope) and latency_time, the event times in seconds.

References

Templeton, E. M., Chang, L. J., Reynolds, E. A., Cone LeBeaumont, M. D., & Wheatley, T. (2022). Fast response times signal social connection in conversation. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 119(4), e2116915119. doi:10.1073/pnas.2116915119

See also

build_network() for every method; build_reverse() for the unweighted replies.

Examples

build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "latency", actor = "Actor",
              action = "Action", time = "Time")
#> Reply Network (response-latency weighted) [directed]
#>   Weights: [0.694, 0.860]  |  mean: 0.741
#> 
#>   Strongest edges (10 of 78):
#>    from       to        weight
#>    monitor    adapt     0.860 
#>    plan       adapt     0.857 
#>    adapt      cohesion  0.821 
#>    coregulate adapt     0.793 
#>    monitor    synthesis 0.792 
#>    discuss    adapt     0.774 
#>    synthesis  plan      0.770 
#>    adapt      plan      0.769 
#>    coregulate synthesis 0.760 
#>    emotion    synthesis 0.755  
#> 
#>   extract_edges(include_self = TRUE) lists every edge; extract_transition_matrix() gives the weight matrix;
#>   extract_initial_probs() the initial probabilities.
#> 
#>   Latency: weight 1 at 0 s, falling to 0.5 at the cap of 476 s (0.95 percentile)  |  mean per pair  |  25533 replies
build_latency(group_regulation_long, action = "Action", time = "Time",
              actor = "Actor")
#> Reply Network (response-latency weighted) [directed]
#>   Weights: [0.694, 0.860]  |  mean: 0.741
#> 
#>   Strongest edges (10 of 78):
#>    from       to        weight
#>    monitor    adapt     0.860 
#>    plan       adapt     0.857 
#>    adapt      cohesion  0.821 
#>    coregulate adapt     0.793 
#>    monitor    synthesis 0.792 
#>    discuss    adapt     0.774 
#>    synthesis  plan      0.770 
#>    adapt      plan      0.769 
#>    coregulate synthesis 0.760 
#>    emotion    synthesis 0.755  
#> 
#>   extract_edges(include_self = TRUE) lists every edge; extract_transition_matrix() gives the weight matrix;
#>   extract_initial_probs() the initial probabilities.
#> 
#>   Latency: weight 1 at 0 s, falling to 0.5 at the cap of 476 s (0.95 percentile)  |  mean per pair  |  25533 replies
